title: Karmic tail 15-8-11 in the destiny matrix: the Devil, the scales and a lion on a chain of flowers

seo.title: 15-8-11 in the destiny matrix: the “Physical Aggression” karmic tail
seo.description: The 15-8-11 karmic tail is not about fists but about a chain: who holds it and what it is made of. Date check, the loop, its cost and the way out per Waite and Wen.

short: 15-8-11 is the karmic tail that popular destiny matrix readings call “Physical Aggression”. The name is scarier than it deserves. The three cards of the tail — The Devil, Justice and Strength — describe not a fight but the way a person handles force, their own and other people’s. The loop goes like this: when order is under threat, the first move is a grip — press, hold on, don’t give way. Then an inner set of scales switches on, and the pressure takes on a lawful look: “I’m within my rights.” The other side answers in kind, and each is sure they were only defending themselves. The task of the tail is Strength in the old sense of the word: not to kill the beast and not to sit on its chain, but to walk it alongside.

sections.h2: The one-minute check: the 15-8-11 tail has one sum — 29
paragraphs: A karmic tail is fully determined by one sum — of the arcana of the day, month and year. The other steps of the formula only unfold it into three cards. For 15-8-11 only one sum works: exactly 29.

ol: **Arcanum of the day.** The day of birth, if it is 22 or less. If it is larger, add its digits: 23 → 5, 25 → 7, 29 → 11, 31 → 4.
**Arcanum of the month.** The number of the month, from 1 to 12.
**Arcanum of the year.** Add the digits of the year; if the result is above 22, add its digits again: 1990 → 19, 1987 → 25 → 7.
**The sum.** Add the three numbers and do not reduce anything. Exactly 29 means your tail is 15-8-11.

paragraphs: Three examples. 25.04.1980: 7 + 4 + 18 = 29 — that is 15-8-11. 03.07.1990: 3 + 7 + 19 = 29 — the same. But 12.04.1975: 12 + 4 + 22 = 38. That sum also reduces to 11 (3 + 8), and the root of the tail is the same, Strength — yet the tail itself comes out different: 6-17-11. The sums 11, 38, 47 and 56 reach Strength by another road, so look at the sum itself, not at what it turns into.
Why exactly 29 works. From there the method’s formula runs the same way for everyone who has it:

This arithmetic gives two facts shared by all 1,951 dates with this tail. First: everyone’s centre of the chart is The Emperor. Apart from 15-8-11, The Emperor sits in the centre of only one tail out of 26, 6-8-20. Second: Manipura, the chakra of will, standing and money, reads the same for everyone — 4-4-8, The Emperor, The Emperor and Justice. What this means is shown below, in the chapters on the arithmetic of power and on work.
The formula gives 15-8-11 for 1,951 dates out of 46,299 between 01.01.1900 and 05.10.2026. That is tenth place among the 26 possible tails. Sex does not affect the numbers.

sections.h2: Where the name “Physical Aggression” comes from, and what is wrong with it
paragraphs: Popular sites retell the same legend. In a past life the soul supposedly had enormous physical strength and used it for evil — in war, in robbery, against those who were weaker. Hence, the legend says, the quick temper in this life, the urge to control and a family that lives in fear. The legend cannot be checked: a date of birth says nothing about past lives, and the calculation method has no step that would.

But the name did not come from nowhere. Copy out the divinatory meanings of the tail’s three cards from Arthur Edward Waite’s The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910), and you get something close to a police report. The Devil’s list opens with **“Ravage, violence, vehemence, extraordinary efforts, force”**. Justice reversed has “bigotry, bias, excessive severity”. Strength reversed has “Despotism, abuse of power”. The vocabulary of aggression really is collected in these cards. There are no reversed cards in the matrix — a calculated number does not lie upside down — but these lists show what a card’s quality turns into when it is bent too far.
Yet the word “physical” is misleading, for three reasons.

The first is frequency. The tail falls on roughly one birthday in twenty-four — about one person in every school class. The portrait of “a tyrant whose family lives in fear” does not fit that share of people. The tail describes something far more ordinary than violence.

The second is Waite himself. His list for The Devil ends with a caveat: **“that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil”**. And his list for Strength opens with “Power, energy, action, courage, magnanimity”. The force in this tail is given. It does not become evil by itself.

The third is form. Force in this tail is rarely physical. More often it is a voice half a tone higher, an ultimatum, checking someone else’s phone, three days of icy silence, money as a leash, a rule invented in the middle of a quarrel. A more accurate name for the tail would be not “Physical Aggression” but “Force Without a Master”. The whole question of 15-8-11 is who holds the chain.

sections.h2: Two chains: the central riddle of the tail
paragraphs: The first and last cards of the tail mirror each other: on both, someone is on a chain. What follows is about what Waite wrote about the cards; the card images on this site are its own, and their details may differ.

On The Devil, Waite describes a man and a woman chained to a ring in front of an altar, and sums up: **“Hereof is the chain and fatality of the material life.”** Next comes a sentence that is usually skipped. The one exalted above the chained pair “is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman, sustained by the evil that is in him and blind to the liberty of service.” In The Devil’s chain both ends are unfree — those who are held and the one who holds.

Strength turns the same composition around. A woman is closing the jaws of a lion, and Waite specifies that her beneficent fortitude **“has already subdued the lion, which is being led by a chain of flowers”**. There is no fight on this card — it ended earlier. Waite explains the chain of flowers as “the sweet yoke and the light burden of Divine Law, when it has been taken into the heart of hearts”. This is a direct echo of the Gospel: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). The lion, in one of Waite’s readings, is the passions, and she who is called Strength is “the higher nature in its liberation”.

Put the two quotations side by side and you get the main discovery about this tail. The Devil is blind to “the liberty of service” — and the Strength card is that very liberty: a chain that was not put on, but taken on by choice. **The root of the tail is exactly what its entry cannot see.** In Waite these cards stand in different chapters and say nothing about each other; the link between them is our reading, but it rests on his own words.

The second echo is in Benebell Wen. In Holistic Tarot (2015), discussing Strength, she recalls a verse from the First Epistle of Peter: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8). So the lion on the Strength card is the very beast that stands at the entry of the tail. 15-8-11 begins with The Devil holding people on a chain and ends with a woman leading a lion on a chain. The beast is the same. What changes is the chain and the hand that holds it.

Hence the main conclusion. The task of the tail is not to get rid of force: without the lion there is no Strength card. Waite says plainly that the card “has nothing to do with self-confidence in the ordinary sense”. It is not about self-assurance or steely endurance but about power over one’s own beast. The question of the tail is not “do I have strength?” but **“whose chain is this, and what is it made of?”**

sections.h2: The arithmetic of power: Strength on a throne becomes the Devil
paragraphs: The numbers of the tail are not independent: each next one is calculated from the previous ones. In 15-8-11 these additions read almost like a parable.

ul: **11 + 4 = 15.** Entry M is the root plus the centre. Strength seated on The Emperor’s throne gives The Devil.
**11 + 15 = 26 → 8.** Mechanism N is the root plus the entry. Strength, having met its own Devil, sits down to judge.

paragraphs: This is our reading of the method’s arithmetic, not a statement by Waite or Wen. But it shows exactly where the tension in the tail comes from: force is not the danger; force that has been given power is.

The centre of the chart is its comfort zone, the state a person returns to when no one demands anything. Everyone with 15-8-11 has The Emperor there. Waite writes of him: “executive and realization, the power of this world” — and adds an important qualification: this is **“the lordship of thought rather than of the animal world”**. The Emperor’s throne is built for the mind, not for the beast. Wen sees in the card “an iron will” and the state where “All is in order, under control.” And straight away she shows the price: she points to the dry rocks behind the throne, asks what the Seeker has actually conquered, and answers: “The kingdom is parched.”

This is how the trigger works. While everything is under control, a person with this tail is calm, composed and reliable. The loop starts when the throne wobbles: someone broke an agreement, disobeyed, decided behind their back. Wen writes that in a conflict The Emperor is a sign of jus ad bellum, the “right to war”: the one who fights is in the right. For 15-8-11 this is the key detail, only seen from the other side: they feel that right in almost every argument. They rarely feel they are attacking. They are restoring order.

There is one more coincidence. Waite uses the same word, “executive”, for two figures — The Emperor and Justice. In the 15-8-11 tail they stand side by side, and at the entry stands The Devil with a chain. Together they make a complete state inside one person: **The Emperor writes the law, Justice passes the sentence, The Devil carries it out.**

In 1748 Montesquieu described where such an arrangement leads. In The Spirit of the Laws he writes that there would be an end of everything if the same person held all three powers — making laws, executing them and judging. And he puts it even more precisely: **“Were it joined to the executive power, the judge might behave with violence and oppression”** (Book XI, chapter 6). The same chapter notes that rulers who wanted to become despots always began by gathering all the powers into their own hands. “Despotism” opens Waite’s reversed list for Strength, and Wen links The Devil with “despotism and enslavement”. One word stands at the entry of the tail and on the underside of its root.

In Russian literature this scheme fits into one line: “I gave thee life, and I will take it!” Gogol’s Taras Bulba is father-lawgiver, judge and executioner at once. The line became a proverb precisely because there is no gap in it between anger, sentence and execution. The 15-8-11 tail almost never goes to Gogol’s extremes. But it is built on the same scheme, and the way out starts with that gap.

sections.h2: How the loop turns: grip, trial, counter-blow
paragraphs: The best portrait of the pair The Devil — Justice was written by Ivan Krylov, Russia’s great fabulist. The wolf in his fable The Wolf and the Lamb (1808) is hungry and could simply eat his prey. But first he holds a trial: “Yet, to give the deed a lawful look and sense, / He shouts: ‘How darest thou, insolent, with thy foul snout / Muddy here the clean water / That is mine…’” The charge does not hold — the lamb is drinking downstream — and the wolf pulls out an old account: “Why, I recall, the summer before last / Thou wast rude to me right here: / I have not forgotten that, my friend!” When even the accounts run out, there comes an honest sentence: **“Thy guilt is simply that I want to eat.”**

Force that needs a lawful look is exactly the mechanism of 15-8-11. The Devil supplies the push, Justice the justification. Without the second, the first would soon burn out: an outburst without a verdict fades; an outburst with a verdict becomes a war. Wen notes in The Devil “a streak of hatred and resentment”, and calls Justice “human-made justice, not divine justice”. In the tail the two meet: the person holds the scales themselves, and the weight on them is their own resentment.

But in real life the person with this tail rarely faces a defenceless lamb. More often it is an equal force — a partner, a boss, a teenager — and then another law applies. Wen explains Justice through Newton’s third law: **“to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction”**. Pressure gives rise to counter-pressure of the same strength, and each side has its own scales: one’s own blow is recorded as a response, the other’s as an attack. In such a loop no one attacks. Everyone is only defending.
The loop goes through six steps:

ol: **The throne wobbles.** Order is under threat: a child broke a rule, a colleague broke an agreement, a partner decided something alone. This is the centre, The Emperor: everything must be under control — and it no longer is.
**The grip.** The first move is The Devil at the entry: press, hold, push it through. Not necessarily with a fist. More often with a voice, an ultimatum, control, silence, money.
**The trial.** The scales switch on: who started it, who owes how much, what happened “the summer before last”. The pressure takes on a lawful look: “I’m within my rights”, “they asked for it”.
**The answer.** The other side answers with the same force — and also in the name of justice, only their own.
**The proof.** The counter-blow confirms the verdict: “See? Being nice doesn’t work with them.” The next round starts at higher stakes.
**The parched kingdom.** Order is restored: the house is quiet, the team obeys. But it is the silence of fear, not of respect — Wen’s kingdom of The Emperor, where there is nothing to drink.

paragraphs: The most vulnerable point of the loop lies between the second and third steps, at the moment the impulse looks for a verdict. As long as anger stays anger, it passes. What makes it dangerous are the words “and that is only fair”.

Here is how it looks on an ordinary evening. At eleven at night a father sees that his son has not done his homework. A minute ago it was just a tired evening. A minute later come the words: “Phone on the table — for a month.” Said at the peak of anger, without discussion, and now it cannot be taken back, because “my word is my word”. The law was never discussed, the trial took a second, the sentence was carried out at once. Three powers in one minute.

sections.h2: The other end of the chain: when the tail is lived in silence
paragraphs: Read only the popular descriptions, and 15-8-11 always seems to be the one who presses. But The Devil’s chain has two ends, and Waite stresses that both are unfree. The tail can also be lived from the end that is held. There are at least three versions.

**The patient one.** Puts up with someone else’s pressure for years — a boss, a parent, a partner — and stays silent. Wen describes the underside of Strength in just these terms: the person holds back their strength, behaves too passively, and the “lion”, the fierce foe, overwhelms them. Meanwhile the scales work without days off: every humiliation is recorded. One day the account overflows, and there is an explosion nobody expected, including the person. After the explosion comes shame — and a new round of patience.

**The one afraid of their own force.** Knows how much anger is inside and so does not argue at all: “better keep quiet, or I’ll say too much”. Force that is forbidden to come out does not disappear. It goes into sarcasm, coldness, clenched teeth.

**The avenger of others.** Does not allow themselves anger on their own behalf, but for someone weaker — that is allowed. Justice issues a licence: “it’s not for me”. Krylov’s wolf, by the way, also tries the lamb for other people’s sins: “But I will settle their sins with thee.”

Wen makes an important caveat about The Devil: the card does not necessarily mean the person is entirely to blame for the position they are in — “the greater culpability rests elsewhere”. For 15-8-11 this means that ending up on the chain is not the same as deserving it. But the way out is the same for the one who holds and the one who is held — Strength. For the first, it is the ability to loosen the grip. For the second, it is the ability not to hand their chain to someone else and to use their own force in time, while it is still calm.

sections.h2: The price: whoever holds the chain is chained to it
paragraphs: The least obvious price of 15-8-11 is hidden in the sentence of Waite’s that is usually skipped: the one who holds the chain is “also a bondsman”. Control cannot be set up and left. It has to be held — checked, reminded, watched so that no one slips out from under the hand. A person who at first only wanted order notices a few years later that they cannot go on holiday, hand over work, let a grown child go. The chain takes up both hands.

The second price is an account that never closes. The scales in this tail cannot reset: every grievance moves to the next round as an argument. Over the years a relationship piles up so many “summers before last” that any quarrel is about everything at once.

The third is the one Wen writes about: the parched kingdom. Things around become quiet and correct, but people either submit or leave. Those close stop arguing — and stop telling. The Emperor stays on the throne alone, but right. In this tail one almost always has to choose between “being right” and “being close”, and the loop chooses the first again and again.

For the one living at the other end of the chain, the price is a mirror image: years of silence after which a single explosion cancels out all the patience. People remember the explosion, not the years.

sections.h2: How the 15-8-11 tail shows up in life
paragraphs: What follows are typical scenes, not predictions. The tail describes a habitual move, not what is bound to happen.

paragraphs.h3: Closeness: The Devil stands at the entry twice

paragraphs: Point M — the entry of the tail — also serves as the entry of the relationship line M–R1–R. So for everyone with 15-8-11, the first reaction in closeness and the first reaction in the old scenario are the same card, The Devil. Relationships become the tail’s main stage. Attraction here is strong and clingy: “mine”, jealousy as a way of holding on, checking a phone as a small trial. The scales keep a tally of contributions: who earns more, who gave in more, who apologised first last time.

For those whose year arcanum is 10 (people born in 1900, 1999, 2008, 2017 and 2026), the relationship line repeats the tail in full: 15-8-11 again. There are 79 such dates out of 1,951, about 4%. For them the “15-8-11 programme” is not only an old scenario but also a way of loving.

The strong version of this scene is loyalty, the ability to protect one’s own and not to run from conflict. A person with this tail can stay in a hard conversation to the end — if there is no verdict in that conversation.

paragraphs.h3: Children: law, trial and punishment in one minute

paragraphs: The scene with the phone and the homework shows what the loop looks like in a family. A parent with this tail sincerely wants order at home and often really does create it. What breaks is not the order but the method: the rule appears at the moment of the violation, the sentence is passed at the peak of anger, the punishment does not wait. In such a system a child easily learns one of two answers — submit or hit back. Both answers are the same chain, simply passed on.
The working version is built differently: the rules are known in advance, so are the consequences, and the decision to punish is not made in the minute when one wants to punish.

In the report Manipura is the chakra of will, standing and money. For everyone with the 15-8-11 tail it reads the same: 4-4-8, The Emperor, The Emperor and Justice. These are the same cards as in the centre and the mechanism of the tail: the theme of power and fair order is sewn into money and status. At work this gives real strengths. Such a person can build a system, keeps their word and demands the same from others, and is not afraid of responsibility.

The shadow is fines instead of conversations, micromanagement, a public dressing-down “as a lesson to the others”, money as a way of deciding for others: “I pay, so I decide.” For 92% of people with this tail, Justice also stands in the social purpose — the point that shows how a person is useful to many. A repeated arcanum does not double, but it shows that the theme of justice in such a chart is not limited to the tail, and its strong version can become a life’s work.

paragraphs.h3: Body and sport: why the ring models the tail done right

paragraphs: Popular advice for 15-8-11 often includes sport, especially combat sports. That advice has an exact basis in the cards themselves. All three elements of the tail are present in the ring: force (The Devil), a referee and rules (Justice), self-command (Strength). But unlike in life, the referee in the ring is another person. The powers are separated, and **force gets a lawful place instead of a lawful look**.

The body usually learns that the loop has started before the head does: a clenched jaw, fists, heat in the face, a voice half a tone higher. Waite’s Strength closes the lion’s jaws — literally its jaws. For someone with 15-8-11, their own jaw is a good first sensor.

sections.h2: Strength or violence: telling them apart by the cards
paragraphs: The same card in this tail can work in two ways. The words in the table come from Waite’s divinatory lists; the split into “loop” and “strength” is ours.

head: Card and role
When the loop is turning
When strength is at work
rows: **extraordinary efforts**: the ability to give everything when it is truly needed
bias, excessive severity, a tally of grievances
**equity, probity**: being right without a verdict
despotism, abuse of power — or strength locked inside
control for the sake of control, a parched kingdom

paragraphs: Four questions help to see where a person is right now:

ul: **Why the pressure?** To regain control — that is the loop. To protect someone weaker — that is strength.
**Who is the judge?** Me, right now — the loop. A rule agreed in advance, or a third person — strength.
**What about the debt?** Collect it with interest — the loop. Forgive it, because one can afford to — strength.
**What comes after?** Silence and obedience — the loop. The argument goes on, but nobody is afraid — strength.

sections.h2: What changes the scenario: nine practices
paragraphs: Waite reminds us that three Tarot cards — Justice, Strength (his other name for it is Fortitude) and Temperance — go back to the cardinal virtues, while the fourth, Prudence, is missing from the deck altogether. The 15-8-11 tail holds two of them: justice and fortitude. What it lacks is measure and prudence, and the practices below essentially make up for exactly these: a pause, order before the conflict, a view from outside.

ol: **Separate the powers.** Do not carry out a decision to punish, fire or break up on the same day it was made. Say: “I’m angry. I’ll decide tomorrow.” The gap between sentence and execution is what Taras Bulba did not have.
**Pass laws in peacetime.** Discuss the rules of the home, the couple, the team while everyone is calm, and write them down. During a quarrel there are no new laws — only consequences already known.

**Hear the wolf in your own speech.** The phrases “they started it”, “I have the right”, “they asked for it”, “I haven’t forgotten that” are a signal that the scales are already turning force into a verdict. Noticing such a phrase means stopping at the third step of the loop, not the fifth.

**Start with the jaw.** When the teeth and fists clench, the force is already in the body. The first action is not a word but a movement: step out, walk, splash water on your face, say “I’ll be back in twenty minutes” — and come back. Without the return, the pause turns into one more punishment, by silence.
**Give the lion a job.** Regular exertion with rules: the ring, the gym, running, heavy work with your hands. Force needs a lawful place, or it will look for a lawful look.

**Ask instead of ordering.** Wen writes of Strength that one cannot use brute force to exercise will over others; one must use gentle, subtle influence. The practice is simple: one request with a reason instead of one order a day.

**Forgive one debt a week.** Deliberately do not collect — a late arrival, a sharp word, an unwashed mug. Magnanimity is in Waite’s list for Strength for a reason: only the strong can afford not to collect.

**Say “no” early.** This one is for those living the tail from the other end of the chain. It is easier to name a boundary calmly the first time than to explode on the tenth. An early “no” is the same Strength, only released in time.
**Choose the role of protector.** Waite’s Emperor also means “protection” and “aid”. Force that defends rather than punishes stops being The Devil, even if it stays just as big.

paragraphs: If force has already turned into blows, threats, broken things or fear at home — on either end of the chain — this is not a destiny matrix question. If anyone is in danger, call your local emergency number or a local crisis line. Psychologists and crisis centres work with repeated violence, and both the one who presses and the one being pressed can turn to them.

sections.h2: The strong version of 15-8-11: power that does not need to roar
paragraphs: The most interesting thing about this tail: when the loop is broken, the force does not go anywhere. What changes is not its amount but its master.

A strong 15-8-11 can be recognised by a few signs. They can stop a fight because they know fights from the inside. They can say a hard truth in a calm voice. They hold a rule without cruelty and drop it if the rule has stopped serving people. In a crisis, when others lose their heads, they pull order together — and after the crisis they hand power back. People listen to them not out of fear but because it is safe to be near them.

All of this is written in the same Waite lists, only on the front side. For Strength: **“Power, energy, action, courage, magnanimity; also complete success and honours”**. For The Emperor: “Stability, power, protection, realization… aid, reason, conviction”. For Justice: “Equity, rightness, probity”. Even The Devil’s upright list includes “extraordinary efforts” — the ability to give everything when it is really needed. Wen has two short formulas for Strength: “Triumph of love over hate” and “Compassion is strength.”

Such force is needed where pressure is part of the job: crisis management, rescue services, coaching, defence in court, negotiation, leadership in hard conditions, raising teenagers. These are examples, not a prediction of a profession.

Waite calls the woman on the Strength card “the higher nature in its liberation”. The path of the 15-8-11 tail runs from a chain put on by others to a chain one chooses oneself. The lion stays the same lion. Only now it walks alongside.
Four other tails are easy to confuse with 15-8-11: they share its entry, its centre or its root.

paragraphs: The most instructive pair is 15-8-11 and 15-5-8. Both tails have The Devil at the entry and both contain Justice, but its roles are opposite. In 15-5-8 justice is the root, the task the tail leads to. In 15-8-11 it is the mechanism that keeps the loop going. The same card can be the way out in one tail and the trap in another.

Permutations — 11-8-15, 8-15-11, 8-11-15 and the rest — are never produced by the tail formula for any date. If such a triple turns up in a reading, it belongs to another position in the chart or another school of calculation, and it cannot be read as 15-8-11.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: **Calculation.** The classic destiny matrix in Natalia Ladini’s method: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M, every sum reduced to 22 or less. The “sum equals 29” rule and all the statistics come from checking every date from 01.01.1900 to 05.10.2026 — 46,299 days.

**Waite.** A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, 1922 reprint): the symbolism of The Devil, Justice, Strength and The Emperor from Part II and the divinatory meanings from Part III. Quotations are given in the original.
**Wen.** Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015), the sections on The Devil, Justice, Strength and The Emperor. Quotations are given in the original.

**Literature.** Ivan Krylov, The Wolf and the Lamb (1808); Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws (1748), Book XI, chapter 6, in Thomas Nugent’s translation; Nikolai Gogol, Taras Bulba. Krylov and Gogol are quoted in our own translation.
**The Bible.** Matthew 11:30 in the King James Version and 1 Peter 5:8 in the wording Wen quotes — as the sources of images that Waite and Wen refer to.

**Our reading.** The link between the two chains, the reading of the arithmetic (11 + 4 = 15, 11 + 15 → 8) and the three-powers scheme are the author’s interpretation, not statements by Waite or Wen. The past-life legend is given as a popular interpretation, not as fact.

faq.q: What happened in a past life to someone with the 15-8-11 tail?
faq.a: The popular legend speaks of great physical strength that the soul used for evil — in war, in robbery, against the weak. This cannot be checked: a date of birth holds no information about past lives. The legend works as a metaphor for force without a master, but not as a biography.

faq.q: Does the 15-8-11 tail mean a person is aggressive or dangerous?
faq.a: No. The tail falls on roughly one birthday in twenty-four and describes a relationship with force, not actions. Many live it from the other end of the chain: they put up with other people’s pressure or are afraid of their own anger. The card does not establish how anyone behaves.

faq.q: Is the 15-8-11 tail different for women and men?
faq.a: The numbers are the same: sex plays no part in the calculation. The differences popular sites describe are more about what kind of anger the people around allow. Some are more easily forgiven for pressing, others only for patience and an explosion on the tenth time. The loop is the same either way: grip, scales, counter-blow.

faq.q: Why do some sites say 8 is Strength and others say it is Justice?
faq.a: In the old Marseille-pattern decks 8 is Justice and 11 is Strength, and the destiny matrix uses this numbering. In 1910 Waite swapped these two cards “for reasons which satisfy myself”, as he puts it, and in decks of his pattern 8 is Strength. The 15-8-11 tail is made of exactly this pair. Read it in Waite’s numbering, and the cards of the mechanism and the root swap places, turning the meaning of the tail upside down.

That is what the same triple is sometimes called in another position. In the matrix it can also appear on the relationship line M–R1–R: such a line falls on 319 dates out of 46,299, about 0.7%. For people born in 1900, 1999, 2008, 2017 and 2026 who have the 15-8-11 tail, the relationship line repeats it completely. The meaning of the triple depends on the position: on the relationship line it is a scenario of closeness, not a karmic task.

faq.q: Can the 15-8-11 tail be “closed” or “worked off”?
faq.a: The numbers of a date do not change; the tail stays in the chart for good. What changes is how it is lived: the loop “grip — trial — counter-blow” opens when law, sentence and enforcement no longer fit into one minute and one pair of hands. The measure is not a feeling of “I’ve worked through it” but the fact that the people around stop being afraid.

ul: **Cards and roles:** 15 The Devil — entry, 8 Justice — mechanism, 11 Strength — root. Everyone with this tail has the same arcanum in the centre of the chart — 4, The Emperor.
**How to tell from a date:** the arcana of the day, month and year add up to exactly 29. The formula knows no other way to this tail.
**How often:** 1,951 dates out of 46,299 since 1900, or 4.2% — roughly one birthday in twenty-four.
**The main trap:** not anger, but force that has found a justification.
**The way out:** put law, judgement and enforcement into different hands — and learn a kind of power that does not need to roar.

report: The hungry wolf in Krylov’s fable could simply have eaten the lamb. But first he holds a trial: “Yet, to give the deed a lawful look and sense…” The charge does not hold, and the wolf pulls out an old account: “I have not forgotten that, my friend!” When even the accounts run out, an honest sentence follows: “Thy guilt is simply that I want to eat.” Force that needs a lawful look is the most precise description of the 15-8-11 tail.

Popular readings call it “Physical Aggression” and explain the name with a legend: in a past life the soul supposedly had enormous strength and used it for evil. The legend cannot be checked — a date of birth says nothing about past lives. But the words for the name really are in the cards. Waite’s divinatory list for The Devil opens with “Ravage, violence, vehemence, extraordinary efforts, force”. On the underside of Justice lie “bias, excessive severity”; on the underside of Strength, “Despotism, abuse of power”.

Still, the word “physical” misleads. Force in this tail rarely raises a hand. More often it is an ultimatum, icy silence, money as a leash, a rule invented in the middle of a quarrel. And Waite ends The Devil’s list with a caveat: **“that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil”**.

report.h3: The root of the tail is what its entry cannot see

report: In Waite’s descriptions the first and last cards of the tail mirror each other: on both, someone is on a chain. About The Devil he has a sentence that is usually skipped. The one exalted above the chained pair “is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman, sustained by the evil that is in him and blind to the liberty of service.” In The Devil’s chain both ends are unfree.

On Strength, Waite says, the lion has already been subdued and is being led by a chain of flowers — “the sweet yoke and the light burden” of a law taken into the heart of hearts. This is the very liberty of service The Devil is blind to. **The root of the tail is exactly what its entry cannot see.**

Benebell Wen, discussing Strength, recalls the verse from the First Epistle of Peter in which the devil “prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour”. The lion on the Strength card is the same beast that stands at the entry of the tail. The beast is one; what changes is the chain and the hand that holds it. So the task of 15-8-11 is not to get rid of force: without the lion there is no Strength card. The task is to decide whose chain it is and what it is made of.

report.h3: Law, trial and enforcement in one pair of hands

report: Everyone with 15-8-11 has The Emperor in the centre of the chart — the comfort zone where all is in order and under control. The loop starts when the throne wobbles: a child broke a rule, a colleague broke an agreement, a partner decided something behind someone’s back. The first move is The Devil at the entry: press, hold, push it through. Then the scales of Justice switch on: who started it, who owes how much. The pressure takes on a lawful look — “I’m within my rights”.

So a whole state assembles inside one person: **The Emperor writes the law, Justice passes the sentence, The Devil carries it out.** In 1748 Montesquieu warned where this leads: “Were it joined to the executive power, the judge might behave with violence and oppression.” In Russian literature the same scheme fits into one line from Gogol’s Taras Bulba: “I gave thee life, and I will take it!” The tail almost never goes to such extremes, but it is built the same way. An ordinary evening: a father sees the homework not done, and a minute later come the words “phone on the table — for a month”. The law was never discussed, the trial took a second, the sentence was carried out at once.

Usually the other side is not a lamb but an equal force. Wen explains Justice through Newton’s third law: to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction. Each side has its own scales — one’s own blow recorded as a response, the other’s as an attack. **In such a loop no one attacks. Everyone is only defending.**

report.h3: Whoever holds the chain is chained to it

report: The price is hidden in the same sentence of Waite’s: the one holding the chain is also a bondsman. Control cannot be set up and left; it has to be held. The scales cannot reset, and every grievance moves to the next round as an argument. Things around become quiet and correct, but people either submit or leave. Wen puts this kingdom of The Emperor briefly: “The kingdom is parched.” In this tail one almost always has to choose between “being right” and “being close”.

The tail is also lived from the other end of the chain. The patient one puts up with someone else’s pressure for years while the scales work without days off, until a single explosion cancels out all the patience. The one afraid of their own force keeps quiet, and the anger goes into sarcasm and clenched teeth. The avenger of others allows anger only when it is “not for me”. The chain is the same; only the end changes.

report.h3: A lawful place instead of a lawful look

report: Of the four cardinal virtues, the tail holds two: justice and fortitude. What it lacks is measure and prudence, and the way out is built from exactly these:

ul: separate the powers: do not carry out a decision to punish or break up on the same day — “I’m angry, I’ll decide tomorrow”;
pass laws in peacetime, and during a quarrel use only the ones already known;
hear the wolf in one’s own speech: “they started it”, “they asked for it”, “I haven’t forgotten that”;
forgive one debt a week: magnanimity is on Waite’s list for Strength, and only the strong can afford it;
for those at the other end of the chain, say “no” early, while the force is still calm.

report: Force needs **a lawful place, not a lawful look**. That is why the ring works so well: it has force, rules and self-command, but the referee is another person. If force has already turned into blows, threats or fear at home — on either end of the chain — this is a matter not for the matrix but for a local emergency number or crisis line, for psychologists and crisis centres.

A strong 15-8-11 can stop a fight because they know fights from the inside, say a hard truth in a calm voice and hand power back once the crisis is over. People listen to them not out of fear but because it is safe to be near them. The path of the tail runs from a chain put on by others to a chain one chooses oneself. The lion stays the same lion. Only now it walks alongside.
